newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: U.S. REPORT ON SLOVAKIA FACILE - SLOVAK DIPLOMAT.
newsitem.headline: U.S. REPORT ON SLOVAKIA FACILE - SLOVAK DIPLOMAT.

text.p: A U.S. government report to congress on NATO expansion is superficial in its assessment of Slovakia's respect for democracy and human rights, a senior Slovak foreign ministry official said on Wednesday.

Emil Kuchar, general director of the ministry's political section, said in an interview with the official TASR news agency that many western countries generalised expressing their doubts about Slovakia's eligibility for NATO membership.
TASR quoted him as saying that the U.S. report was very superficial, at least in the part concerning candidates.

"A dialogue consists not only of one side formulating its reeservations," Kuchar said. "What is important is the degree to which the other side is willing to listen to our arguments and the results of such a discussion."

President Bill Clinton's report on NATO enlargement last month widely details aspects of the planned enlargement of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, analysing the 11 former communist countries which have expressed interest in joining.

Slovakia objected to a reference in the U.S. report which said that in the field of respect for basic human rights "serious problems have been noted in some (countries), such as Albania and Slovakia..."

Kuchar said Slovakia was as well-prepared for NATO membership as other leading candidates such as the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary and had no wish to base its individual dialogue with NATO on pointing out the mistakes of other candidates, TASR reported.
Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's nationalist-populist coalition government has declared membership in NATO and the European Union as its top foreign policy priorities.
Meciar has repeatedly said he wants Slovakia to be one of the first of the former Soviet bloc countries to join NATO.

NATO member states are to hold a summit in Madrid in July to nominate the first candidates for membership from post- communist countries. Diplomats have said Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic are most likely to be named.
NATO has said that basic criteria for membership include sufficient development of democracy, respect for human rights and the transformation to an open market economy.

Soon after the split of Czechoslovakia in 1993, Slovakia was considered among the top contenders for early NATO entry, but in recent years the United States and the EU repeatedly criticised Bratislava for lagging behind in the development of democratic principles.

Most often diplomats from Brussels and Washington have listed as problematic Bratislava's official treatment of ethnic minorities, restrictions on press freedom, and tolerance for political opposition positions.
Washington's reservations on Slovakia were repeated by John Kornblum,, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for European and Canadian Affairs, during a lecture in Bratislava last week.
"In our analysis there are questions on Slovakia and it appears that Slovakia has fallen out of the mainstream, but we are still not stating preferences," Kornblum said.
"Diversity, openness and tolerance are the way to a prosperous society. But we are concerned that this message is not being heard loud enough (in Slovakia)," he added.
